title: Red-Teaming Auto Mode: Improving Blocking Classifiers Against Malign Coding Agents
summary: Red-Teaming Auto Mode: Improving Blocking Classifiers Against Malign Coding Agents Alignment Science Blog Red-Teaming Auto Mode: Improving Blocking Classifiers Against Malign Coding Agents Alex Remedios 1* , Simon Storf 1* October 22, 2026 Fabien Roger 2 , John Hughes 2 1 Anthropic Fellows Program; 2 Anthropic * Primary contributors. Name order randomised. tl;dr We red-team production blocking monitors (Auto Mode in Claude Code, Guardian in OpenAI’s Codex) with an adversarial agent in an experimental setting with the objective of improving the safety of coding agents. Our most effective attack strategies bypass the monitor using agent-generated prompt injection against the monitor, multi-agent attacks, or malicious compaction. We attempt to improve the robustness of auto-mode by improving tool coverage, transcript formatting and using an agentic monitor stage. We find that robustly preventing multi-context attacks at an acceptable cost remains an open problem. 📝 Paper , 💻 Code Research done as part of the Anthropic Fellows Program . Introduction Coding agents can now run for days with little or no human involvement, completing software tasks end to end ( Kwa et al., 2025 ). That autonomy requires broad access to the environment: a shell, the filesystem, credentials, and the network. title: How Depth Growth and Looping Shape In-Context Learning in Language Models
summary: Looped and depth-grown language models reuse computations across depth and have attracted interest for their reasoning capabilities. Building on prior suggestive evidence of improved in-context-learning (ICL), we investigate how such reuse favors ICL, including how it shapes the acquisition, retention, and mechanisms of this ability. Our analysis spans pretrained language models up to 3B parameters and controlled tasks. The experiments provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context: grown and looped models rely more on information in context and, compared with a full-depth dense reference, acquire ICL earlier in controlled tasks and retain it more strongly when learning fixed associations in the weights is also possible. Tracing attention heads through training reveals that depth growth propagates early induction heads across layers. Ablations show that grown and looped models rely more strongly on induction-ranked heads for both few-shot performance and later-token prediction. Together, these findings provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context and suggest that (soft) parameter reuse shapes how this ability develops and which attention mechanisms support it.

title: Red-Teaming OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring Systems
summary: For three weeks, from July 21st to August 11th, a METR employee and a Redwood Research employee conducted a pilot high-access exercise to stress-test OpenAI’s internal misalignment monitoring system. 1 The output of this exercise was a 61-page internal report that was shared with OpenAI researchers and security staff, 2 primarily focused on estimating the fraction of agentic inference that is monitored, and whether agents could in principle disable or subvert the monitoring system. The exercise focused on the internal misalignment monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21st, and did not evaluate changes that were in progress at the time of the exercise. This exercise involved a deep level of access. The METR and Redwood employees had access to OpenAI’s internal codebase, misalignment-monitor prompts / configuration details, and internal documentation, and conducted technical interviews with approximately a dozen researchers and engineers across the monitoring, safety-systems, and security teams. To enable this level of access, they worked on OpenAI-issued devices, which never left the premises, and were accompanied while onsite. METR, Redwood Research, and OpenAI designed this exercise as a pilot for giving external researchers deep access to internal infrastructure, not to provide robust public transparency about OpenAI’s monitoring systems. 3 As a result, we agreed upfront with OpenAI that we would only publish a relatively brief and high-level public post. title: Monitorability evaluations and policy proposals
summary: There has been a lot of discussion recently of policy proposals around monitorability, such as Redwood's proposal and my counter-proposal . I'd like to say a bit more generally about how I'm thinking about monitorability. Note that nothing here is an official Anthropic position; these are just my personal thoughts. First, a categorization. I currently think about four different types of monitorability: Control Monitorability: the extent to which Control and monitoring techniques would likely catch catastrophic sabotage actions, like escaping a sandbox or setting up a rogue internal deployment. We can measure this via reference to sabotage evaluations like LinuxArena or any evaluation that measures the model’s capability to take dangerous actions like escaping a sandbox while looking to a monitor like it's doing some innocuous task (like a cyber eval). Training Monitorability: the extent to which reward models, monitors, and oversight in training would likely catch misaligned or undesirable actions in training, such as sneaky/subtle reward hacks. Auditing Monitorability: the extent to which alignment audits, evaluations, and test deployments would likely incriminate a systematically misaligned model (e.g. a schemer)—as well as the extent to which monitor evaluations would likely detect a model's propensity to collude as a monitor. title: BeNice! Closing Looping's Inference-Memory Gap via KV-Sharing
summary: Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers. During inference, each recurrence generates independent KV-caches, causing memory to grow linearly. To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth), finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences without quality loss, a property we denote as KV-shareability. However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it. In this paper, we study how KV-shareability can be enabled in looped models. We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use stochastic depth during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence's KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model's quality. As a result, BeNice! enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning's unshared validation perplexity. Using BeNice!, we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g., fp8, mxfp8, nvfp4). Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.
